title: Childhood lead poisoning: conservative estimates of the social and economic benefits of lead hazard control.
ehr_evidence: Data for children with BLLs < 10 μg/dL are estimated from CDC NHANES 2003–2006. Data for > 10 μg/dL are from state-level surveillance and assume uniform distribution of cases within each BLL group.
summary: Cost-benefit analysis quantifying the social and economic benefits of household lead paint hazard control compared to investment costs for children ≤ 6 years in the US.
key_findings: Each dollar invested in lead paint hazard control results in a return of $17–$221 or a net savings of $181–269 billion.
Total costs of lead hazard control range from $1.2 to $11.0 billion, while total benefits range from $192 to $270 billion.
Lead exposure is associated with 9.3–13.1 million points of IQ loss, translating to $165–233 billion in lost lifetime earnings.
data_source_type: NHANES survey data and state surveillance data
population: children ≤ 6 years of age in the United States
limitations: restricts analysis to lead-based paint as the primary source
uses conservative lower bounds for prevalence
excludes indirect crime costs and long-term adult health effects
assumes uniform distribution of BLLs within groups
small sample sizes prevent accurate categorizing of children into each BLL subgroup
